_about: Plain-language copy for the report pages (render_report.py). Written for a tenth-grade reader: short sentences, no code names, no file paths. Every rule in rules.json needs an entry here. title = the problem as a person would say it; why = why it matters on the phone; fix = what to do; passed = the rule stated as something that already works; ask = the question a person answers when the rule needs a human check. after = what the After frame of the Prototype tab shows once the fix is applied (one string, or one per platform); hidden = why a listed problem has no After on a screen. Every rule with a patch in capture_after.mjs needs an after. prototype = every other word on the Prototype tab.

IOS-NAV-01.title: The tab bar is custom-built
IOS-NAV-01.why: iPhone users expect the standard tab bar. The built-in one floats over the page with a glass look, shrinks as you scroll, and works with VoiceOver without extra work.
IOS-NAV-01.passed: The app uses the system tab bar
IOS-NAV-01.after: The tab bar becomes iPhone's floating glass bar, with a label under every icon. A web page can only hint at the glass.
IOS-NAV-01.hidden: No tab bar shows on this screen as captured.

IOS-NAV-02.title: The tab bar has too many tabs, or a tab acts like a button
IOS-NAV-02.why: iPhone tab bars hold up to 5 places to go. A tab that does an action instead, like opening a form, surprises people.
IOS-NAV-02.fix: Keep 5 tabs or fewer, and move actions out of the tab bar.
IOS-NAV-02.passed: The tab bar has 5 tabs or fewer, and no tab acts as a button

IOS-NAV-03.title: Search sits in the page, not where iPhone puts it
IOS-NAV-03.why: When search is a main task, iOS 27 gives it its own tab or puts it in the top bar. That is where people look for it.
IOS-NAV-03.fix: Give search its own tab, or put it in the top bar.
IOS-NAV-03.passed: Search sits where iPhone users look for it
IOS-NAV-03.ask: Is searching a main task on this screen? If it is, iPhone expects search in its own tab or in the top bar.

IOS-NAV-04.title: A hamburger menu is the main way to get around
IOS-NAV-04.why: iPhone users expect a tab bar at the bottom. A hidden side menu makes the main places harder to find.
IOS-NAV-04.fix: Use a tab bar for the main places in the app.
IOS-NAV-04.passed: No hamburger menu is used as the main navigation

IOS-NAV-05.title: The back button is custom-built
IOS-NAV-05.why: The standard back button also lets people swipe from the left edge to go back, or press and hold to jump back further. A custom button loses both.
IOS-NAV-05.fix: Use the system back button in the top bar.
IOS-NAV-05.passed: Screens use the system back button
IOS-NAV-05.after: The custom back button becomes a plain chevron in its own glass circle, the way iPhone draws it.
IOS-NAV-05.hidden: No back button shows on this screen as captured.

IOS-BAR-01.title: The top bar has a solid background
IOS-BAR-01.why: On iOS 27, the page scrolls under a see-through top bar and the system softly fades the edge. A solid bar blocks that.
IOS-BAR-01.fix: Make the top bar see-through and let the page scroll under it.
IOS-BAR-01.passed: Top bars let the page scroll under them
IOS-BAR-01.hidden: This only shows when the page scrolls under the top bar.

IOS-BAR-02.title: The top bar has too many buttons
IOS-BAR-02.why: More than 3 buttons in the top bar crowd it and make each one harder to hit.
IOS-BAR-02.fix: Keep 3 buttons or fewer, and move the rest into a “more” menu.
IOS-BAR-02.passed: Top bars show 3 buttons or fewer

IOS-BAR-03.title: The “…” button does only one thing
IOS-BAR-03.why: On iPhone, “…” means “more options.” People expect a short list, not a new page.
IOS-BAR-03.fix: Give the button its own icon or a word, like “Details.”
IOS-BAR-03.passed: The “…” button is only used for more options
IOS-BAR-03.ask: Does the “…” button open a list of more options, or does it do just one thing?

IOS-GLS-01.title: Glass is stacked on top of glass
IOS-GLS-01.why: Two see-through layers on top of each other make text and icons hard to read.
IOS-GLS-01.fix: Keep one glass layer. Make the inner part solid.
IOS-GLS-01.passed: Glass is never stacked on top of glass

IOS-GLS-02.title: Cards or rows use a glass look
IOS-GLS-02.why: On iPhone, glass is for bars and controls that float over the page. On cards and rows it makes the page busy and harder to read.
IOS-GLS-02.fix: Give cards and rows a solid background.
IOS-GLS-02.passed: Glass is used on bars and controls, not on cards
IOS-GLS-02.ask: Is the blurred surface a bar or control that floats over the page, or a card or row in the page?

IOS-GLS-03.title: Text on see-through surfaces is hard to read
IOS-GLS-03.why: Some people make glass clearer, and some turn transparency off. Text has to stay readable in both cases.
IOS-GLS-03.fix: Check text on glass at every glass setting and fix any that fades.
IOS-GLS-03.passed: Text on see-through surfaces stays readable

IOS-MNU-01.title: Main actions are hidden in a menu
IOS-MNU-01.why: People shouldn't have to open a menu to do the main thing on a screen.
IOS-MNU-01.fix: Show main actions as buttons. Keep menus for less-used actions.
IOS-MNU-01.passed: Main actions are not hidden inside menus
IOS-MNU-01.ask: Does the menu button in the top bar hide something people need to do often on this screen?

IOS-MNU-02.title: A menu has fewer than 3 items
IOS-MNU-02.why: A menu with one or two items adds a tap for no reason.
IOS-MNU-02.fix: Show one or two actions as buttons instead of a menu.

IOS-MNU-03.title: Menus are custom-built
IOS-MNU-03.why: iPhone's built-in menus grow out of the button you tapped, use the glass look, give a small vibration and work with VoiceOver.
IOS-MNU-03.hidden: The menu is closed in this view, so there is nothing to show.

IOS-MNU-04.title: Pick-one choices don't show which one is picked
IOS-MNU-04.why: When people choose one option, like a sort order, they need to see which one is on.
IOS-MNU-04.fix: Show a checkmark next to the current choice.
IOS-MNU-04.passed: Pick-one controls show which option is picked

IOS-MNU-05.title: Some actions are only in a press-and-hold menu
IOS-MNU-05.why: Many people never press and hold. An action that only lives there is hidden from them.
IOS-MNU-05.fix: Put every press-and-hold action somewhere on screen too.
IOS-MNU-05.passed: Nothing can be reached only by press-and-hold
IOS-MNU-05.ask: Can everything in the press-and-hold menu also be done from a button on screen?

IOS-MNU-06.title: An action that ends something has no warning and isn't red
IOS-MNU-06.why: Actions that end or delete something should be red and ask “Are you sure?” first, so nobody taps them by accident.
IOS-MNU-06.fix: Show the action in red and confirm it with a short dialog.
IOS-MNU-06.passed: Actions that end or delete something are red and ask first
IOS-MNU-06.ask: Is this action red, and does it ask “Are you sure?” before it ends or deletes something?
IOS-MNU-06.hidden: The menu is closed in this view, so there is nothing to show.

IOS-SHT-01.title: Pop-up panels are custom-built
IOS-SHT-01.why: iPhone's built-in sheets open to half or full height, can be dragged, and get the new glass look. Custom panels miss all of this.
IOS-SHT-01.fix: Use a system sheet that opens to medium or large height.
IOS-SHT-01.passed: Pop-up panels use the system sheet
IOS-SHT-01.after: The panel sits in from the screen edges, with rounder corners and a grabber, like an iPhone sheet.
IOS-SHT-01.hidden: The pop-up panels are closed in this view, so there is nothing to show.

IOS-LAY-01.title: Buttons sit under the notch or the home bar
IOS-LAY-01.why: The top and bottom edges of the iPhone are covered by the camera area and the home bar. Buttons there are hard or impossible to tap.
IOS-LAY-01.fix: Keep buttons inside the safe area. Only backgrounds should reach the edges.
IOS-LAY-01.passed: Buttons stay clear of the notch and the home bar
IOS-LAY-01.ask: On a real iPhone, do any buttons sit under the camera area at the top or the home bar at the bottom?

IOS-TYP-01.title: Text doesn't grow with the iPhone's text size setting
IOS-TYP-01.why: Many people turn up the text size in Settings. Text set to a fixed size stays small for them.
IOS-TYP-01.fix: Use Apple's text styles, like Body and Headline, so text follows the person's setting.
IOS-TYP-01.passed: Text grows with the iPhone's text size setting
IOS-TYP-01.hidden: Text that grows with the reader's size setting can't be shown in one picture.

IOS-ICN-01.title: Bar icons aren't Apple's SF Symbols
IOS-ICN-01.why: SF Symbols match the system's text weight and size, so bars that use them look native.
IOS-ICN-01.fix: Use SF Symbols for icons in the tab bar, top bar and menus.
IOS-ICN-01.passed: Bar icons use Apple's SF Symbols
IOS-ICN-01.hidden: SF Symbols are Apple's own icons, so a web mock-up can't draw them.

IOS-TGT-01.title: Some buttons are too small to tap easily
IOS-TGT-01.why: Apple asks for tap areas of at least 44 by 44 points. Smaller ones are easy to miss, especially for people with large fingers or shaky hands.
IOS-TGT-01.fix: Make each tap area at least 44 by 44 points. The icon can stay small; only the area you can tap needs to grow.
IOS-TGT-01.passed: Every button is at least 44 by 44 points
IOS-TGT-01.after: Dashed boxes show each tap area grown to at least 44 by 44 points where there is room.

AND-NAV-01.title: The navigation bar is custom-built
AND-NAV-01.why: Android users expect the standard navigation bar, with a pill that shows where you are. A custom bar looks and behaves differently from every other app.
AND-NAV-01.fix: Use the Material navigation bar with 3 to 5 places.
AND-NAV-01.passed: The app uses the Material navigation bar
AND-NAV-01.after: The tab bar becomes Android's navigation bar. It runs edge to edge, every tab has a label, and a pill sits behind the current tab.
AND-NAV-01.hidden: No tab bar shows on this screen as captured.

AND-NAV-02.title: The navigation bar is the older, taller kind
AND-NAV-02.why: Android replaced the tall bottom bar with a shorter one that leaves more room for the page.
AND-NAV-02.fix: Use the shorter bar, 64 dp tall.
AND-NAV-02.passed: The navigation bar is the newer, shorter kind
AND-NAV-02.after: The bar is now the shorter 64 dp navigation bar.
AND-NAV-02.hidden: No tab bar shows on this screen as captured.

AND-NAV-03.title: Tablets and foldables get the phone layout
AND-NAV-03.why: On wide screens, Android expects a side rail and a layout that uses the extra room. Android 17 no longer lets apps opt out of resizing.
AND-NAV-03.fix: At 600 dp and wider, swap the bottom bar for a side rail and widen the layout.
AND-NAV-03.passed: Wide screens get a side rail and a wider layout

AND-NAV-04.title: The back button is custom-built
AND-NAV-04.why: Android has its own back gesture with a preview of where you'll land. A custom back button, or code that blocks back, breaks it.
AND-NAV-04.fix: Rely on the system back gesture. If the top bar shows a back arrow, use the Material arrow, not a chevron or the word “Back.”
AND-NAV-04.passed: Screens use the system back gesture and arrow
AND-NAV-04.after: The custom back button becomes Android's standard back arrow at the start of the top bar.
AND-NAV-04.hidden: No back button shows on this screen as captured.

AND-NAV-05.title: A hamburger menu is the main way to get around
AND-NAV-05.why: Android no longer uses a side drawer as the main navigation on phones. People expect a bar at the bottom.
AND-NAV-05.fix: Use the navigation bar, and a side rail on wide screens.
AND-NAV-05.passed: No hamburger menu is used as the main navigation

AND-BAR-01.title: The top bar has too many buttons
AND-BAR-01.why: More than 3 icons in the top bar crowd it and make each one harder to hit.
AND-BAR-01.fix: Show 3 icons or fewer, and move the rest into a ⋮ menu.
AND-BAR-01.passed: Top bars show 3 icons or fewer

AND-BAR-02.title: The top bar uses iPhone-style word buttons
AND-BAR-02.why: Android top bars use icons, like a check or an X, instead of words like Edit, Done or Cancel.
AND-BAR-02.fix: Use icon buttons in the top bar, or a button in the page.
AND-BAR-02.passed: Top bars use icons, not iPhone-style word buttons

AND-EDG-01.title: The app doesn't reach the edges of the screen
AND-EDG-01.why: Android 16 and later draw every app behind the status bar and the gesture bar. The app has to pad its content so nothing hides under them.
AND-EDG-01.fix: Draw to the edges and pad content by the system bar sizes.
AND-EDG-01.passed: The app reaches the screen edges and pads for the system bars

AND-MNU-01.title: An iPhone-style action sheet shows on Android
AND-MNU-01.why: Android shows choices in a menu next to the button, or in a bottom sheet with a drag handle. An iPhone action sheet looks out of place.
AND-MNU-01.fix: Use a Material menu or a bottom sheet on Android.
AND-MNU-01.passed: Choices use Android menus or bottom sheets
AND-MNU-01.hidden: The menu is closed in this view, so there is nothing to show.

AND-MNU-02.title: Menus are custom-built
AND-MNU-02.why: The standard Android menu has rounded corners, groups, selection marks and its own motion. A custom menu misses these.
AND-MNU-02.hidden: The menu is closed in this view, so there is nothing to show.

AND-MNU-03.title: The “more” button uses a sideways “…”
AND-MNU-03.why: On Android, “more options” is three dots stacked up and down (⋮). The sideways dots are the iPhone version.
AND-MNU-03.hidden: No “…” button shows on this screen in this state.

AND-MNU-04.title: Pick-one choices don't show which one is picked
AND-MNU-04.why: When people choose one option, like a sort order, they need to see which one is on.
AND-MNU-04.fix: Show a check or a radio button next to the current choice.
AND-MNU-04.passed: Pick-one controls show which option is picked

AND-MNU-05.title: The main “add” action has no floating button
AND-MNU-05.why: When adding something is the main job of a screen, Android puts it in a floating button near the bottom, where the thumb is.
AND-MNU-05.fix: Put the add action in a floating button, or a floating button with a short menu.
AND-MNU-05.passed: Screens where adding is the main job have a floating add button
AND-MNU-05.ask: Is adding something the main job of this screen? If it is, Android expects a floating add button.
AND-MNU-05.after: The add action moves out of the page and becomes a floating button near the bottom.
AND-MNU-05.hidden: The add action isn't visible in this view.

AND-SRC-01.title: Search is a plain box in the page
AND-SRC-01.why: When search is a main task, Android uses a search bar at the top: a thick pill with the menu icon and your picture outside it.
AND-SRC-01.fix: Use the Material search bar at the top of the screen.
AND-SRC-01.passed: Search uses the Material search bar
AND-SRC-01.ask: Is searching a main task on this screen? If it is, Android expects the Material search bar at the top.
AND-SRC-01.after: Search moves out of the page and becomes the search bar at the top. The title or logo gives up its spot on this screen.
AND-SRC-01.hidden: No search field shows on this screen as captured.

AND-DYN-01.title: The bars don't pick up the phone's colors
AND-DYN-01.why: Android can tint apps from the person's wallpaper. Keeping your brand colors is fine; this is only something to consider.
AND-DYN-01.fix: Think about tinting the bars from the phone's colors. Keeping brand colors is a valid choice.
AND-DYN-01.passed: The bars pick up the phone's colors, or keep brand colors on purpose

AND-ICN-01.title: Icons use Apple's style on Android
AND-ICN-01.why: Android has its own icon set, Material Symbols. Apple's icons look out of place there.
AND-ICN-01.after: The icons in the bars switch to Material Symbols.
AND-ICN-01.hidden: No tab bar or top bar icons show on this screen as captured.

AND-CTL-01.title: iPhone-style controls show on Android
AND-CTL-01.why: Switches, segmented controls and scrolling pickers look different on Android. The iPhone versions feel foreign there.
AND-CTL-01.fix: Use Material controls on Android: the Material switch, button groups, and menus or dialogs instead of scrolling wheels.
AND-CTL-01.after: The switch takes Android's shape: a wider track, and a thumb with a check when it is on.
AND-CTL-01.hidden: No switch shows in this view. Other controls, like segmented buttons, are not drawn yet.

AND-SHT-01.title: Pop-up panels are custom-built
AND-SHT-01.why: Android's standard bottom sheet has a drag handle and familiar motion. Custom panels miss these.
AND-SHT-01.fix: Use the Material bottom sheet with a drag handle.
AND-SHT-01.passed: Pop-up panels use the Material bottom sheet
AND-SHT-01.after: The panel takes Android's sheet shape: rounder top corners and the standard drag handle.
AND-SHT-01.hidden: The pop-up panels are closed in this view, so there is nothing to show.

AND-TGT-01.title: Some buttons are too small to tap easily
AND-TGT-01.why: Android asks for tap areas of at least 48 by 48 dp. Smaller ones are easy to miss, especially for people with large fingers or shaky hands.
AND-TGT-01.fix: Make each tap area at least 48 by 48 dp. The icon can stay small; only the area you can tap needs to grow.
AND-TGT-01.passed: Every button is at least 48 by 48 dp
AND-TGT-01.after: Top bar buttons are now 48 dp wide and small buttons grow to 40 dp tall. Dashed boxes show each new tap area.

X-PAR-01.title: iPhone and Android get the same custom tab bar
X-PAR-01.why: Neither phone gets the navigation its users already know.
X-PAR-01.fix: Share the screens' content, but give each platform its own native navigation.
X-PAR-01.passed: Each platform gets its own native navigation

after.ios: iPhone gets a tab bar of its own here. Android would get a separate one built for Android.
after.android: Android gets a navigation bar of its own here. iPhone would get a separate one built for iPhone.

X-PAR-01.hidden: No tab bar shows on this screen as captured.

X-PAR-02.title: Navigation parts are the same on iPhone and Android
X-PAR-02.why: iPhone and Android handle tabs, sheets and menus differently. One shared version fits neither well.
X-PAR-02.fix: Give navigation and menus an iPhone version and an Android version.
X-PAR-02.passed: Navigation and menus have a version for each platform

after.ios: You can see this in the new tab bar. The pop-up panels stay closed in this view.
after.android: You can see this in the new navigation bar. The pop-up panels stay closed in this view.

X-PAR-02.hidden: This is about the tab bar and pop-up panels. Neither shows on this screen as captured.

X-PAR-03.title: An action exists on one phone but not the other
X-PAR-03.why: People on both phones need to be able to do the same things, even if the button sits in a different place.
X-PAR-03.fix: Make every action available on both platforms.
X-PAR-03.passed: The same actions are available on both phones

X-PAR-04.title: Both platforms use the same icon set
X-PAR-04.why: iPhone uses SF Symbols and Android uses Material Symbols. One shared set looks a little off on both.
X-PAR-04.fix: Use SF Symbols on iPhone and Material Symbols on Android.
X-PAR-04.passed: Each platform uses its own icon set

after.android: The icons in the top bar and navigation bar switch to Material Symbols.

hidden.ios: SF Symbols are Apple's own icons, so a web mock-up can't draw them.
hidden.android: No tab bar or top bar icons show on this screen as captured.

X-PAR-05.title: Confirmations use a custom pop-up
X-PAR-05.why: The phone's own alert already has the right look, focus handling and screen reader support.
X-PAR-05.fix: Use the native alert or dialog for confirmations.
X-PAR-05.passed: Alerts and confirmations use native dialogs

destinations.name: Main navigation
destinations.ios: A floating glass tab bar with up to 5 tabs. Search can have its own tab.
destinations.android: A navigation bar with 3 to 5 places and a pill for the current one. A side rail on wide screens.

secondary.name: Other buttons on the screen
secondary.ios: Buttons in the top bar, grouped on glass. Less-used ones go in a “more” menu.
secondary.android: Up to 3 icons in the top bar, with a ⋮ menu for the rest.

overflow.name: More options
overflow.ios: Use “…” only to open a list of more options.
overflow.android: A ⋮ button that opens a Material menu.

per-item.name: Actions on one item
per-item.ios: Press and hold an item for a menu. The same actions also appear on screen.
per-item.android: A visible icon on the item that opens a menu. Press and hold selects items.

choose-one.name: Pick one option
choose-one.ios: A button that shows the current choice and opens a list with a checkmark.
choose-one.android: A menu with a check on the current choice, or a row of 2 to 5 buttons.

create.name: Add something new
create.ios: A “+” button. It opens a short menu if there are 3 or more things to add.
create.android: A floating add button, with a short menu if there are 2 to 6 things to add.

destructive.name: Ending or deleting something
destructive.ios: Red text, plus a dialog that asks you to confirm.
destructive.android: A dialog that asks you to confirm, with the action set apart in its own group.

rich.name: Panels with lots of options
rich.ios: A system sheet that opens to half or full height.
rich.android: A bottom sheet with a drag handle.

search.name: Search
search.ios: A search tab, or a search field in the top bar.
search.android: A search bar at the top: a pill with the menu icon and your picture outside it.

account.name: Account
account.ios: A top-bar button that opens a sheet or menu.
account.android: Your picture in the search bar or top bar, opening a menu or sheet.
